It supplies one polynomial-time implementation for the language, with perfect completeness and soundness error $1/2$.

The address bound supplies the finite prefix used by the converse (Theorem 1.2), even when the proof oracle is presented as a function on all natural numbers.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement supplies one verifier, its polynomial-time implementation, three constants and a polynomial before quantifying over inputs. Its conclusions are exactly the randomness, query, address, completeness and soundness conditions listed after this sentence.
rows.name: PCP.np_subset_pcp
rows.annotation: The witnesses to the outer existential include both `V` and the machine algorithm. The resource constants and `p` are fixed at that point, so none may depend on the particular input or the proof.

rows.name: PCP.np_subset_pcp
rows.annotation: For each yes-input, `CompleteAt` chooses a proof before the acceptance probability is computed. Since every seed in the finite space has positive mass, the proof passes every seed. On a no-input the probability bound applies to each proof separately.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement concludes membership in NP from a polynomial-time implementation, the exact logarithmic randomness formula, a polynomial address bound, perfect completeness and soundness error $1/2$. The query bound is already fixed in the verifier.

rows.annotation: A polynomial-time checker can store the `ReadsBelow` prefix and test all seeds. The exact logarithmic formula makes the enumeration polynomial, and a positive soundness gap guarantees a rejecting seed for every candidate on a no-input.

rows.fidelity_note: The paper bounds the zero fraction by $d/q$ when $\deg P\le d$; the formal statement uses the sharper bound $\deg P/q$ for every nonzero polynomial $P$. Substituting $\deg P\le d$ gives the quoted estimate.

rows.annotation: Over a field of size $q$, the polynomial $(X-a)(Y-b)$ vanishes on two coordinate lines, giving fraction $(2q-1)/q^2\le2/q$. The degree bound generalizes this control to polynomials whose zeros have no simple geometric description. The verifier applies it to residuals such as $M(X,Z_H(X))-A(X)$ so that one nonzero residual forces many random evaluation failures.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement gives exactly one extension of individual degree at most $h-1$ for every function on a nonempty grid. The paper works over a finite field, while this result holds over any field with a finite nonempty set $H$.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.GridInterpolation.existsUnique_extension
rows.plain: Unique extension from a nonempty grid
rows.annotation: For $H=\{0,1\}$, the indicator of the grid point $(1,0)$ extends to $X(1-Y)$, which has degree one in each variable and total degree two. Products of the one-variable indicators extend an arbitrary grid table by linear combination. This supplies the colour and adjacency degree bounds and makes the reduced remainder zero in the certificate lemma.

rows.fidelity_note: The display states that encoding halves the distance between two field-valued functions, measured over all labels in $\mathcal B_r$. The formal statement proves exactly this for $r\ge1$, with field values read through any injective coordinate map, which covers the fixed map $\rho$.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.Hadamard.relativeDistance_encodeFunction_map
rows.annotation: At a point where $g$ and $h$ differ, injectivity gives a binary coordinate label on which their values differ. Adding that label pairs agreeing queries with disagreeing queries. The premise $r\ge1$ ensures the coordinate label is available.

rows.fidelity_note: The paper states that (B1) also holds over homogeneous labels. The formal statement proves it for functions with values in $\mathbb F_2^t$: over points paired with homogeneous labels, the encodings are at half the distance of the functions. Applied to $\rho\circ g$ and $\rho\circ h$, with $\rho$ injective, this is the paper's claim.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.Hadamard.relativeDistance_homogeneous_queries
rows.annotation: For messages $(1,0)$ and $(0,0)$, adding the first coordinate label pairs the two homogeneous labels with first coefficient zero with the two having first coefficient one. Exactly half separate the messages. The same pairing at each point where two field values differ gives the distance identity on the very labels sampled by the difference check.

ties.name: PCP.Verifier.ImplementedBy
ties.plain: Verifier steps reproduce each query tree

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition requires the bounded unfolding of the implementation to equal the verifier’s entire query tree for every input and seed. The unfolding includes both possible answers at every query and rejects a further query when its depth is exhausted.
rows.name: PCP.Verifier.ImplementedBy
rows.plain: Verifier steps reproduce each query tree
rows.annotation: If the first proof bit steers a tree to address two or address five, an implementation could agree on the first path and compute the second address incorrectly. Soundness ranges over proofs that take either path. Equality of the whole bounded tree transfers its acceptance and address guarantees to the machine on every input and seed.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition unfolds the next-step procedure for a fixed number of queries, branching on both possible answers. At depth zero it preserves a verdict and turns a request for another address into rejection, as the paper describes.
rows.name: PCP.QueryTree.ofStep
rows.annotation: At an internal node, `ofStep` recurses on the two histories obtained by appending zero and one. At depth zero it preserves a verdict and turns a further request into rejection, so every path meets the depth bound.

rows.fidelity_note: The paper concludes that the amplified verifier runs on a polynomial-time machine. The formal statement proves that the concrete amplified query algorithm is polynomial-time in the machine model of Section 2.3. The cost, storage and repetition bounds named in the sentence are the route of its proof, not separate conclusions.
rows.name: PCP.Lang.ThreeColorRuntime.polyTimeAlg
rows.annotation: `polyTimeAlg` concerns the concrete machine cost of the query computation, including the work between reads. The constant query count alone would give no bound on that cost. The storage and repetition estimates enter in the proof of this machine-level assertion.

rows.fidelity_note: In characteristic two, the formal statement assumes $u^3=v^3=1$ and proves $(u-v)^3=1$ if and only if $u\ne v$. These are the hypotheses satisfied by the two colours in the surrounding argument.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorAlgebra.sub_cube_eq_one_iff_ne
rows.annotation: In $\mathbb F_4$, $1+\omega=\omega^2$. Two vertices labelled $1$ and $\omega$ have nonzero difference with cube one, whereas two vertices labelled $\omega$ have difference zero. The fourth-power identity extends this calculation to the cube roots of unity in the paper's larger fields. The edge polynomial can then use a cube equation to require distinct colours.

rows.fidelity_note: The paper describes the constraints of the particular colouring extension $P$ and recovers a colouring from that same polynomial. The formal statement instead equates colourability with existence of some $P$ of degree at most $m(h-1)$ satisfying both constraints; the correspondence for a given $P$ is proved separately.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorGrid.colorable_iff_exists_constraints
rows.annotation: `colorable_iff_exists_constraints` turns the fixed-polynomial argument into an existence theorem with the additional degree cap. Interpolation (Lemma 2.2) gives that cap for the extension of a colouring, and restricting any polynomial satisfying both identities gives the reverse implication.

rows.fidelity_note: For the given polynomial $P$, the formal statement proves that $A_P$ vanishes on $H^m$ and $B_P$ on $H^{2m}$ exactly when the grid values of $P$ satisfy $x^3=1$ at every vertex and $(P(a)-P(b))^3=1$ on every edge. rows.plain: Grid vanishing encodes both colouring constraints
rows.annotation: The `edgeExtension` evaluates to one on grid edges and zero on grid nonedges, so the edge polynomial vanishes exactly when the edge equation holds on each edge. `Satisfies` also includes the separate vertex equation.

rows.fidelity_note: In characteristic two, the formal statement shows that the vertex and edge equations hold exactly when every value is a cube root of unity and adjacent vertices receive distinct values. This is the step of Lemma 3.1 used in the converse; it says nothing about $A_P$ or $B_P$ themselves.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorAlgebra.satisfies_iff
rows.annotation: The hypothesis that all vertex values cube to one permits `sub_cube_eq_one_iff_ne` to turn each cubic edge equation into inequality of the endpoint values. The equivalence is about field assignments to vertices before identifying the roots with the three named colours.

rows.fidelity_note: For a primitive cube root of unity $\omega$, the formal statement shows that the solutions of $x^3=1$ are exactly $1,\omega,\omega^2$, the three colour values. It supplies the last step from distinct cube roots of unity to a proper three-colouring.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorAlgebra.cube_eq_one_iff
rows.plain: Colours as cube roots of unity
rows.annotation: The primitive root gives three distinct candidates $1,\omega,\omega^2$. The cubic has at most three roots in a field, so these exhaust its solutions and identify the values allowed by the vertex equation.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement equates grid vanishing with existence of a certificate of degree at most $\deg A$ satisfying the two substitution identities. The quoted lemma additionally states a decomposition into $Z_H(X_i)U_i$ and a converse for certificates of any degree; those are separate results used in the proof.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.GridVanishing.vanishesOn_iff_exists_certificate
rows.annotation: The degree ceiling on the certificate is needed to encode its honest line restrictions below the digit cutoff (Lemma 3.3). On the grid the two identities alone force $A(X)=M(X,0)=0$. The nonempty-grid premise lets the forward construction retain the degree ceiling.

rows.fidelity_note: The lemma's first sentence is an equivalence. The formal statement proves its forward direction: a polynomial vanishing on $H^k$ equals $\sum_iZ_H(X_i)U_i$, with the extra bound $\deg U_i+|H|\le\deg A$ for each nonzero $U_i$. The easy reverse direction and the certificate identities are not part of it.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.GridVanishing.exists_decomposition
rows.annotation: Take $H=\{0,1\}$ and $A(X,Y)=(X^2-X)Y$. Dividing by $Z_H(X)=X^2-X$ gives quotient $Y$ and zero remainder. Replacing the divisor by a new variable turns the degree-three summand into a degree-two certificate term. In general the paper needs the uniform quotient-degree bound so the certificate's line restrictions fit within the honest encoding cutoff.

rows.fidelity_note: This is the lemma's last sentence: any polynomial $M$ with $M(X,0)=0$ and $M(X,Z_H(X_1),\ldots,Z_H(X_k))=A(X)$ forces $A$ to vanish on $H^k$, with no condition on the degree or shape of $M$. It does not give the decomposition or the existence of a certificate.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.GridVanishing.IsCertificate.vanishesOn
rows.annotation: Under the two identities, a grid point makes every coordinate of $Z_H(X)$ zero, so the value of $A$ is zero there. This direction places no restriction on the degree of $M$ or its degree in the certificate variables.

The verifier uses this operation to check the derived constraint without an additional proof table.

rows.annotation: This instance uses the repetition count chosen for the graph verifier. Conditional on one fixed proof, the seeds are independent, so accepting all repetitions multiplies the acceptance probabilities. Each repetition reads within the original address bound.

rows.annotation: `np_subset_pcp` closes the runtime premise and records the full resource bounds for the source language. The reduction preserves the yes or no status, so the graph verifier’s completeness and soundness clauses apply to the corresponding original input.

ties.name: PCP.finiteWitnessCheck
ties.plain: Checking a witness on every seed

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition is the witness relation described here: it accepts an input and a finite bit string exactly when the verifier, reading the string as a proof with every later bit zero, accepts on every random seed.
rows.name: PCP.finiteWitnessCheck
rows.plain: Checking a witness on every seed
rows.annotation: The NP checker must accept one candidate proof prefix on every random seed. Lean’s `oracleOfWitness` reads the list at an in-range address and gives zero otherwise. `finiteWitnessCheck` wraps the universal test over the finite seed type in `decide` to return a Boolean. The address bound makes padding irrelevant for a full prefix, and the separate machine and seed bounds make the enumeration polynomial-time.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement shows that the first $N$ bits of a proof, read back as a proof, agree with the original at every address below $N$. With $N=p(n)$ this is why taking the first $p(n)$ bits as the witness preserves every run; the sentence names the truncation, not this fact.
rows.name: PCP.oracleOfWitness_prefix
rows.annotation: `oracleOfWitness_prefix` requires $j<N$. Combined with `ReadsBelow`, it gives equality at every address along the verifier’s adaptive execution, so replacing the oracle by its prefix does not change a verdict on any seed.

rows.fidelity_note: With the verifier assumptions of Theorem 1.2, the formal statement establishes that the language has a polynomially bounded witness relation computable in polynomial time. The proof uses the relation that accepts a finite proof prefix exactly when every seed accepts.
rows.name: PCP.pcp_subset_np_concrete
rows.annotation: The converse supplies a polynomial-time implemented witness checker, as well as the equivalence with membership. The finite-prefix bound controls witness length, while the number of seeds controls the extra simulation cost.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement proves both directions between the project’s polynomial-time witness-checker definition of NP and the reference nondeterministic-machine definition. It requires no additional machine simulation or cost hypothesis from the reader.
rows.name: PCP.ReferenceNP.inNP_iff_mem
rows.annotation: `inNP_iff_mem` applies in both directions for every language. It lets a reference NP membership hypothesis enter the verifier construction and identifies the concrete witness class produced by the converse (Theorem 1.2) with the same reference class.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement assumes $q>2d$ and that every affine-line restriction of $f$ is represented by a polynomial of degree at most $d$. It then constructs a polynomial of total degree at most $d$ representing $f$ everywhere, in any finite dimension.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.PolynomialLine.exists_polynomial_of_hasLowDegreeLines_finite
rows.annotation: The premise is that every affine-line restriction has low degree. The field-size inequality in the multivariate characterization prevents a high-total-degree function on the finite grid from having all of its line restrictions represented at degree at most $d$.

rows.fidelity_note: With nonzero nodes and $(2n^2+3n)\delta<1$, the formal statement proves that the plurality correction satisfies every weighted constraint. Neither distinct nodes nor nonzero weights are required, in agreement with the lemma.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.WeightedConstraint.correction_satisfies
rows.annotation: The numerical premise makes a union of the exceptional slope choices have probability below one, so there is a choice on which the weighted predictions for the correction identity all agree. Nodes need only be nonzero for the sampling changes of variables used here.

rows.fidelity_note: For generator nodes over a finite field with $q>2c$, the formal statement gives a polynomial of total degree at most $c$ within distance $2\delta$ whenever rejection is at most $\delta<1/[2(c+2)^2]$. There is no characteristic-two restriction in this result.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.GeneratorLowDegreeTest.exists_close
rows.annotation: Generator nodes serve two roles. With their Lagrange weights they give the test identity, and the generator powers let exact solutions be identified along lines. The small-error premise is used to turn plurality correction into such an exact solution.

rows.fidelity_note: The display bounds the corrector's error at every target $u$ by $(c+1)\eta$ over a uniform slope. The formal statement proves this for every $P$ of total degree at most $c$, every function $f$ and every $u$, assuming the correction nodes are distinct and nonzero, as Lemma 4.5 does just before (A13).
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.StandardLocalCorrection.failure_le
rows.annotation: For a fixed $u$, each point $u+a_i v$ is uniform when the slope is uniform because $a_i$ is nonzero. Distinct nodes give exact interpolation for the polynomial. A union bound on the $c+1$ sampled positions gives the estimate even at an atypical target.

ties.name: PCP.Algebraic.LineTableLocalCorrection.correct_wrong_le
ties.plain: Bound on accepted wrong line corrections

rows.fidelity_note: The display bounds the probability of accepting with an output other than $P(u)$ by $\eta+d/(q-1)$, for the procedure of Lemma 4.6 with a uniform slope and a uniform nonzero parameter. The formal statement proves this bound for any lines table of degree at most $d$, any $P$ of degree at most $d$ and any point $u$. It gives no lower bound on acceptance.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.LineTableLocalCorrection.correct_wrong_le
rows.plain: Bound on accepted wrong line corrections
rows.annotation: An incorrect supplied line value at the target makes the supplied restriction different from the polynomial’s true restriction. They can coincide at at most $d$ parameters. A bad point-table read costs at most $\eta$ because a uniform slope at each nonzero parameter gives a uniform queried point. The estimate is for wrong acceptance.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement constructs $P$ of degree at most $d$ in each variable with distance at most $4\varepsilon$. It uses $d>0$, $q\ge1000d^3$, row and column errors at most $\varepsilon\le1/100$, and arbitrary degree-$d$ approximants, exactly as in Theorem 4.7.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.BivariateAgreement.exists_polynomial_of_row_column_agreement
rows.annotation: The row and column approximants can be chosen independently. Their separate small-distance premises, with the field large enough for the reconstruction, force one polynomial of degree at most $d$ in each variable to be close to the entire table.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement selects $10d$ distinct columns, each with row–column discrepancy at most $1/10$, from the two global error bounds, $\varepsilon\le1/100$ and $q\ge20d$. It does not require the degree bounds on the row or column polynomials used in the surrounding theorem.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.BivariateColumnSelection.exists_good_columns
rows.annotation: The sum of the two global errors bounds the mean disagreement between rows and columns. Markov’s inequality leaves enough columns with discrepancy at most $1/10$ to choose $10d$ distinct ones. Polynomial degrees play no role in this selection.

rows.fidelity_note: The display bounds the degrees in $Y$ of $E$ and $N$ by $(5d+1)d$. From enough close rows, the formal statement constructs a nonzero $E$ and an $N$ satisfying the identities (A17), with degree in $Y$ at most $(d+2e+1)D$ for error allowance $e$ and column degree $D$; $e=2d$ and $D=d$ give $(5d+1)d$. It also bounds the degrees in $X$.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.BerlekampWelchCertificate.exists_certificate_of_good_specializations
rows.annotation: The formal certificate comes from solving the row interpolation equations with room for an error locator of degree $e$. Determinant degree bounds in the column variable give $(d+2e+1)D$, which yields the display at $e=2d$ and $D=d$.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement selects $d+1$ distinct columns on which $E$ is a nonzero polynomial. It uses $E\ne0$, the bound $\deg_X E\le2d$, more than $3d$ selected nodes and individual degrees below $q$; the preceding construction and field bound provide these conditions.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.BivariateCleanRectangle.exists_nonzero_columns
rows.annotation: Choose a nonzero coefficient of $E$ when expanded in $Y$. If a column specialization vanishes identically, its node is a root of that coefficient as a polynomial in $X$. The degree cap thus leaves at least $d+1$ usable columns.

rows.fidelity_note: The paper uses the particular coarse bound $\rho\le\varepsilon+1/9$. The formal statement gives the same conclusion $\Delta(f,P)\le4\varepsilon$ for any supplied coarse bound $\rho$ satisfying $\rho+\varepsilon+2d/q\le1/3$, together with the stated degree and row–column error bounds.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.BivariateAgreementBoost.distance_le_four_mul
rows.annotation: The coarse closeness bound (Equation (A19)) is used to show that disagreeing degree-$d$ slices cannot occur too often. The threshold involving $2d/q$ accounts for the possible roots of a difference on a row and a column. Adding the original table-to-row error yields $4\varepsilon$.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement gives a polynomial of total degree at most $d$ within twice the actual whole-field test rejection probability, assuming $q\ge10^6d^3$ and rejection at most $1/4{,}000{,}000$. It includes degree zero, dimension zero and arbitrary received line polynomials of the stated degree.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.PointLineTest.exists_close_of_small_rejection
rows.annotation: The comparison parameter ranges over the whole field. Neither the line table nor its indexing is assumed consistent. Under the field and rejection bounds the conclusion gives one polynomial on the point domain, including when the degree or domain dimension is zero.

rows.fidelity_note: The display bounds, at every fixed parameter $t$, the probability over $u,v$ that $f(u+tv)$ differs from the nearest line polynomial at $t$ by $4\delta'$, under the condition $q\ge3d$ stated just before it. The formal statement proves this for the table of nearest degree-$d$ line polynomials, with $\delta'$ that table's rejection probability.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.PointLineTest.rejectionAt_le_four_mul
rows.annotation: When a line’s mean error is below $1/3$, the nearest degree-$d$ polynomial is unique under $q\ge3d$. Shifting the base point then shifts that polynomial, which compares the error at a fixed parameter with the mean error. The fraction of lines above the uniqueness threshold is at most $3\delta^\prime$.

rows.fidelity_note: The paper’s crossing lemma derives a nearby bivariate polynomial from the row and column errors. This formal statement instead assumes a polynomial within distance $\rho$ and uses $2(\varepsilon'+\varepsilon+\rho+d/q)<1-d/q$; taking $\rho=4\varepsilon$ and $\varepsilon'=\varepsilon$ supplies the step used in the proof.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.PointLineCrossing.crossing_eq_of_nearby_polynomial
rows.annotation: Given a nearby bivariate polynomial, the proof compares its slices through the crossing with the two selected approximants. If a slice differs, low degree forces disagreement outside a small root set. The numerical premise makes that much disagreement impossible under the supplied global and crossing errors.

rows.fidelity_note: The paper requires nearestness only for the two polynomials at the selected crossing. The formal statement uses nearest polynomials on every row and column; it proves the crossing equality for that more restricted choice, with separate global and crossing error bounds.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.BivariateCrossingSoundness.crossing_bestApproximation_eq
rows.plain: Nearest row and column polynomials agree
rows.annotation: `crossing_bestApproximation_eq` chooses nearest approximants along every row and column, then evaluates two at the selected crossing. The global bounds make a nearby bivariate polynomial available and the additional crossing bounds let the proof identify the two selected values.

ties.name: PCP.Algebraic.CandidateCrossing.crossing_eq
ties.plain: Candidate row agrees with nearest column

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement allows arbitrary degree-$d$ row and column families, with the selected row within $\varepsilon$ of its row and only the selected column required to be nearest. The five error bounds, $q\ge1000d^3$, $d>0$ and $6\varepsilon+2d/q<1/2$ give equality at the crossing.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.CandidateCrossing.crossing_eq
rows.plain: Candidate row agrees with nearest column
rows.annotation: The selected row only has to be close to the received row. The nearestness requirement is on the selected column, where the corresponding slice of the nearby bivariate polynomial can be used as a competitor. This is the asymmetric form used in the ruled-surface argument.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement concludes that every affine line of $g$ is exactly represented by a polynomial of degree at most $d$. It needs the displayed distance, endpoint, fixed-parameter and exceptional-event bounds, but does not require the input lines table to consist of nearest polynomials.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.RuledSurface.hasLowDegreeLines_of_endpoint_bounds
rows.annotation: The comparison polynomial is chosen once for the fixed line. For each point on it, the endpoint and crossing estimates allow a ruled surface on which the candidate and the corrected function agree at that point. This gives a degree-$d$ representation of every line even for an arbitrary input lines table.

rows.fidelity_note: From $d>0$ and $q\ge10^6d^3$, the formal statement gives the two quoted bounds and also $q\ge3d$, $q>2d$ and $6/100+2d/q<1/2$. These additional conclusions justify the later uses of the line and crossing estimates.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.PointLineConstants.field_bounds
rows.annotation: The single premise $q\ge10^6d^3$ supplies the bivariate field bound (Theorem 4.7), the conditions for reparametrization and line characterization, and the numerical crossing inequality (Equation (A26)). Positive $d$ is what yields the absolute floor of $10^6$.

rows.fidelity_note: The paper gives the numerical upper bound $0.482025$ and hence a value below one. The formal statement proves only that the same exceptional-event expression is strictly below one under $q\ge10^6$ and $\delta'\le1/4{,}000{,}000$; the sharper decimal is a calculation in the prose.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.PointLineConstants.rigidity_budget
rows.annotation: A bound strictly below one is enough to choose a ruled surface avoiding all exceptional events. `rigidity_budget` proves that strict inequality using the field and rejection thresholds. The decimal in the paper is a sharper evaluation of the same bound.

rows.fidelity_note: For any degree-zero lines table, the formal statement constructs a constant polynomial within twice the test’s rejection probability. It assumes neither a minimum field size nor a small rejection probability, and includes dimension zero as the paper states.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.PointLineTest.exists_close_degree_zero
rows.annotation: Draw two independent uniform points. If their values differ, at least one disagrees with any single proposed constant that is compared to both. Using parameters $t$ and $t+1$ on a random indexed line supplies such a pair and a common constant. Hence the disagreement probability is at most $2\delta$, and some fixed value from the second point is within that distance of the received function. This handles degree zero without the positive-degree field-size argument.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition substitutes $Y^{kb^i}$ for the variable indexed by $(i,k)$, exactly as displayed. It is defined over any commutative semiring of coefficients, so neither a field nor finiteness is needed.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.SetMultilinear.decode
rows.annotation: Decoding substitutes $Y^{k b^i}$ for the variable in group $i$ with digit $k$. This produces a univariate polynomial before any value is assigned to $Y$. In Lean, the paper’s base $b$ is named `m`. `decode` is a ring homomorphism built with `MvPolynomial.eval₂Hom`, which applies `Polynomial.C` to coefficients and substitutes the displayed powers of `Polynomial.X` for variables.

rows.fidelity_note: For $b\ge1$ and $\deg p<b^c$, the formal statement proves the polynomial identity $\Psi(p)\circ\Phi=p$. The paper works over a finite field, while the identity holds over any commutative semiring of coefficients.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.SetMultilinear.decode_encode
rows.annotation: With base two and three positions, $6=0\cdot1+1\cdot2+1\cdot4$. The term $Y^6$ encodes as $X_{0,0}X_{1,1}X_{2,1}$ and polynomial substitution sends it to $1\cdot Y^2\cdot Y^4$. The identity holds coefficient by coefficient below $2^3$, which gives a left inverse even over a ring where two distinct polynomials can agree at every point.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement proves injectivity of $\Psi$ on polynomials of degree strictly below $b^c$, assuming $b\ge1$. It holds for any commutative semiring of coefficients, not only for the finite field used in the paper.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.SetMultilinear.encode_injective_on
rows.annotation: On the restricted degree range, `decode` is a left inverse of `encode`. Applying it to an equality of two encodings proves equality of the original polynomials, with the degree hypotheses on both originals used for recovery.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement gives $\Psi(p)(\Phi(z))=p(z)$ at every $z$ when $\deg p<b^c$ and $b\ge1$. It holds over any commutative semiring of coefficients; the field and finiteness assumptions in the paper are unnecessary for this identity.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.SetMultilinear.eval_encode
rows.annotation: `eval_encode` evaluates the polynomial identity at the supplied point. The strict degree cutoff ensures that the digit representation is complete, so the same calculation applies at zero and at every other point.

rows.fidelity_note: The display says that the composed label $\Lambda_{A,L}$ reads the bit $L(A(u))$ from the degree-$r$ encoding of $u$. The formal statement proves this identity for every $u$, every univariate $A$ of degree at most $r$ and every affine label $L$, with the fixed coordinate map $\rho$.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.HadamardComposition.encode_query
rows.annotation: An affine observation of $A(u)$ can be evaluated by one label on $u$. Field multiplication is bilinear in binary coordinates, and reducing powers at binary inputs gives a multilinear label of degree at most $r$.

ties.name: PCP.Algebraic.BLR.exists_linearMap_distance_le_of_rejection_le
ties.plain: BLR rejection bounds distance to linearity

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement supplies a linear functional within distance $\epsilon$ whenever the binary linearity test rejects with probability at most $\epsilon$. It holds for every rejection probability and every finite binary vector space, including dimension zero.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.BLR.exists_linearMap_distance_le_of_rejection_le
rows.plain: BLR rejection bounds distance to linearity
rows.annotation: The conclusion gives a linear functional on the space of labels, with no small-error threshold. A linear functional on labels need not be evaluation at a binary message. The unit and product tests in Theorem 5.2 are what later enforce that extra property.

rows.fidelity_note: The paper uses a binary linear functional and obtains error at most $2\epsilon$ at every requested label. The formal statement gives the same two-query estimate for any homomorphism between additive commutative groups with a finite input group, using twice the actual distance from the received word.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.Hadamard.selfCorrect_failure_le
rows.annotation: Translating by the requested label preserves the uniform distribution of the mask. The homomorphism property cancels the shift, so only the two events where a read differs from the homomorphism contribute to the error. This argument works for an arbitrary additive target group as in the statement.

ties.name: PCP.Algebraic.Hadamard.test_soundness
ties.plain: Hadamard soundness on two label sets

rows.fidelity_note: For $r\ge1$ and rejection at most $\epsilon<1/28$, the formal statement supplies one binary vector with full-label distance at most $\epsilon$ and affine-label distance at most $3\epsilon$. The fixed coordinate isomorphism converts that vector into the field element $u$ in the paper.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.Hadamard.test_soundness
rows.plain: Hadamard soundness on two label sets
rows.annotation: Read Sudan’s Probabilistically Checkable Proofs, Lecture 3, §§2.5–2.6, in order. First recover the answer at a fixed Hadamard label from a uniform mask and its translate. Then ask which words would pass every linearity check if the labels included products of coordinates. That question leads to the extra checks in the theorem here. A linear functional on quadratic labels could send $1$ to one, both $Z_1,Z_2$ to zero and $Z_1Z_2$ to one. Linearity alone allows that assignment, but the product check compares one with $0\cdot0$. The test uses such checks to recover evaluation at one message. Its affine comparison also controls the error on affine labels for that same message, which is used when the verifier takes weighted sums.

rows.fidelity_note: The display gives one function $g$ whose encoding is within $28\overline e$ of $w$ over all labels and over homogeneous labels. The formal statement proves that such a $g$ exists for every table $w$ and every $r\ge1$, with both bounds for the same $g$ and no small-error assumption.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.Hadamard.exists_field_function_of_average_rejectionRate
rows.annotation: A field value is chosen for each row, and the row bounds are averaged over points. High-error rows can be assigned any value because their rejection cost times $28$ is already at least one. This gives both distances for the same field-valued function without claiming it is a polynomial.

rows.fidelity_note: With $q>2c$, generator nodes and $r\ge1$, the formal statement constructs one degree-$c$ polynomial whose encoding is within $K_c\kappa$ of the received table over both full and homogeneous labels. There is no restriction on $\kappa$, as the paper states.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalRowDecoding.exists_polynomial_distance_le
rows.annotation: The result upgrades rowwise field decoding to one polynomial using the weighted low-degree test. Both distances use the same polynomial, and the constant is large enough to cover rejection above the range of the small-error theorem (Theorem 4.4) by the trivial bound on distance.

rows.fidelity_note: The display bounds by $(c+1)\tau$ the probability that the corrected bit (B12) differs from $L(U(u))$, over a uniform slope and a uniform homogeneous label. The formal statement proves this at every fixed target $u$ for $U$ of total degree at most $c$ and distinct nonzero correction nodes, averaged jointly over slope and label; it gives no bound for a fixed label.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.BinaryStandardLocalCorrection.failure_le
rows.annotation: For each nonzero correction node the evaluation point is uniform under a uniform slope. A nonzero interpolation weight permutes the homogeneous labels, so each sampled read has error bounded by the homogeneous distance. The estimate averages over the label as well as the slope.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement proves the bound $2r+2c+12$ for every seed and $r\ge1$. It needs no generator, distinct-node or field-size assumption, unlike the conditions used for soundness in the surrounding section.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.EncodedLineLowDegreeTest.queries_length_le
rows.annotation: The length bound counts the queries in the binary point-versus-line test at an arbitrary seed. Interpolation nodes can be passed to the query construction even when they fail the geometric hypotheses needed to prove its verdict reliable.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement gives acceptance on every seed for the honest tables when $\deg P<b^c$. It only requires distinct test nodes and distinct nonzero correction nodes; the generator and field-size conditions used elsewhere in the section are unnecessary for completeness.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.EncodedLineLowDegreeTest.test_eval
rows.annotation: The honest restriction has degree below $b^c$, so substituting at $\Phi(z)$ in its encoded polynomial gives the true line value. Distinct test nodes and distinct nonzero correction nodes suffice for the exact evaluations at every seed.

ties.name: PCP.Algebraic.EncodedLineLowDegreeTest.exists_close
ties.plain: One low-degree polynomial, both label domains

rows.fidelity_note: The display bounds both the full-label and the homogeneous-label distance of the points table $f$ from $\mathcal H_r(P)$ by $S_c\kappa$, with $S_c=28+J_c$. The formal statement proves that some $P$ of total degree at most $D$ satisfies both bounds, assuming $q\ge10^6D^3$, $J_c\kappa\le1/4\,000\,000$ and the node conditions of the section.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.EncodedLineLowDegreeTest.exists_close
rows.plain: One low-degree polynomial, both label domains
rows.annotation: The small-error premise is on the comparison between the decoded lines and the decoded point function. The resulting point polynomial is used for both distance bounds. The $28$ term in $S_c$ comes from decoding the original point rows (Corollary 5.3).

ties.name: PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.run
ties.plain: Testing line consistency before binary correction

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition first tests the selected line entry, compares its corrected bit at $\Phi(z)$ with the points table, and returns the corrected bit at $\Phi(0)$ only if both checks pass. The two corrections use the same inner slope and homogeneous label, with $z\ne0$.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.run
rows.plain: Testing line consistency before binary correction
rows.annotation: A proposed line can hit the true value at a sampled nonzero parameter while having the wrong intercept. The corrector first tests the received row and checks one of its predicted bits against the points table. If both checks pass, it returns the row's predicted bit at the intercept. This lets the verifier ask about a prescribed certificate point while checking the prediction at a uniformly distributed point.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition evaluates that procedure on the product sample consisting of the outer slope, nonzero parameter, inner slope, homogeneous label and inner-test seed. Uniform sampling of this product gives precisely the independent choices described in the paper.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.sample
rows.plain: Binary correction on a full seed
rows.annotation: To correct at a fixed target $a$, the procedure uses a random line through $a$ and compares a predicted bit elsewhere on that line. In Lean, `sample` unpacks the product seed into the outer slope, nonzero parameter, inner slope and homogeneous label, and inner-test seed. It passes them to `run`, whose `Option` result is either rejection or a bit. The nonzero-parameter type ensures that for each parameter the uniform outer slope gives a uniform comparison point.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement bounds the number of proof-bit queries of the corrector by $3c+9$ for every seed, every target and every choice of nodes, as the sentence states.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.queries_length_le
rows.annotation: The query list includes the inner row test, the point comparison and the predictions at both inner targets. Its uniform length bound $3c+9$ is also valid for received tables that fail the consistency checks.

ties.name: PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.run_eval
ties.plain: Honest tables give the requested bit

rows.fidelity_note: For $P$ of total degree below $b^c$, given its honest points table and lines table, the formal statement proves that the corrector returns $L(P(a))$ on every seed. It assumes distinct test nodes and distinct nonzero correction nodes, which the sentence does not repeat.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.run_eval
rows.plain: Honest tables give the requested bit
rows.annotation: For an honest line table, `eval_encode` identifies the inner polynomial at the two special points with the outer restriction at $z$ and zero. Exact interpolation supplies both bits, so the returned optional value is `some` of the intended observation for every seed.

ties.name: PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.failure_le
ties.plain: Binary correction failure at fixed targets

rows.fidelity_note: The quote ends before the bound. The formal statement bounds rejection or a wrong returned bit by $C_c\kappa_a+\delta+D/[2(q-1)]$, with homogeneous-label distance at most $\delta$, $D\ge cb^c$ and the stated node conditions; the probability averages over the label as well as the other samples.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.failure_le
rows.plain: Binary correction failure at fixed targets
rows.annotation: Subtract the true restriction from a proposed line polynomial. A wrong intercept makes the difference a nonzero polynomial of degree at most $D$, and among $q-1$ nonzero parameters at most $D$ can hide the discrepancy at the field-value level. The homogeneous label sees half the remaining discrepancies. This accounts for $D/[2(q-1)]$ in the failure bound, alongside the local retest cost and the average points-table error.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement gives (B22), obtained from (B21) by division by the positive number $1+2C_c$. Its assumptions include nonempty $H$, $D\ge cb^c$, both polynomial degree bounds, the homogeneous-label distance bounds and the stated node conditions, so the two displayed inequalities are equivalent here.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.BinaryZeroOnGridCorrection.rejectionRate_ge
rows.annotation: Lean divides the grid inequality by $1+2C_c>0$ to bound the rejection rate itself. The two correction calls (each controlled by Equation (B16)) give the factor two on certificate-table distance. Substituting the grid vanishing polynomials can increase degree by a factor of $|H|$, which explains the field-size term.

topics.description: Polynomial-time verification with logarithmic randomness and a constant number of proof-bit queries characterizes NP.
